pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** The Digestive System

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'Animals, including humans'):** "describe the simple functions of the basic parts of the digestive system in humans".

- **Standards — US (no direct NGSS PE at this band):** NGSS treats the digestive system as one of the interacting subsystems in MS-LS1-3 (middle school), and structure/function survival roles in 4-LS1-1; there is no elementary PE naming digestive organs. Treat as UK-led and note the later US placement.

- **Operational details:** Children trace the journey of food along the alimentary canal as a sequence of organs with SIMPLE functions: mouth (teeth break up food, saliva begins to soften/break it down), oesophagus (muscular tube that squeezes food down to the stomach), stomach (churns food and mixes it with acids/juices), small intestine (nutrients are absorbed into the blood), large intestine (water is absorbed), rectum and anus (waste leaves). The organising idea is a one-way processing pipeline: food is progressively broken down so useful nutrients can be absorbed and waste removed. Keep functions 'simple' — no enzymes or villi detail yet (that is KS3).

- **Operational details continued:** Best taught by physically modelling the journey (mashing a biscuit as 'teeth', squeezing food through a tights-tube as peristalsis) so the sequence and the transformations are enacted, not just labelled.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/sequential). A Y4 child can order the organs and state each organ's simple job; the transitional stretch is understanding that the small intestine ABSORBS nutrients into the body (not just 'passes food along') and that the stomach doesn't 'digest everything' by itself.
bestPractices: Model the journey physically: mash a cracker with a fork as 'teeth', add water as 'saliva', squeeze the mush through a leg of tights as peristalsis — so the transformations are enacted before they are labelled.

Organise the whole topic as a one-way sequence and keep functions SIMPLE (mouth breaks up, stomach churns, small intestine absorbs nutrients, large intestine absorbs water) — defer enzymes and villi to KS3.

Explicitly teach 'absorb' as nutrients LEAVING the tube and entering the blood, using a picture of particles crossing the small-intestine wall, so children don't think food merely passes straight through.
Distinguish the small intestine (absorbs nutrients) from the large intestine (absorbs water) directly, because children routinely conflate them.
Connect teeth-as-mechanical-breakdown here to the parallel Y4 'types of teeth' topic so the mouth is understood as the first digestion stage.
Use accurate but child-friendly organ positions on a body outline so children locate the stomach (upper left, not the belly button) and the long coiled intestines correctly.
keyRepresentations: A body-outline diagram with the alimentary canal drawn as a continuous labelled tube from mouth to anus
A 'journey of the food' flow sequence with an icon and one-line job for each organ
A peristalsis model (food squeezed along a flexible tube) showing muscular movement
A close-up of the small-intestine wall with nutrient particles crossing into a blood vessel (what 'absorb' means)
A hands-on mashing/tights model that mirrors mechanical breakdown and peristalsis
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the stomach does all the digesting and absorbing, rather than most nutrient absorption happening in the small intestine.
Believing food 'just passes through' unchanged, missing that it is progressively broken down and that useful nutrients cross into the blood.
Confusing the small and large intestines — or assuming 'small' means less important — rather than small intestine = nutrient absorption, large intestine = water absorption.
Placing the stomach at the belly button, or imagining a single bag where all food sits, instead of a long connected canal.
Thinking the oesophagus works by gravity ('food falls down') rather than by muscular squeezing (peristalsis), which is why you can swallow lying down.

learn.summary: For 8–9 year-olds (UK DfE Y4 'Animals, including humans'): describe the simple functions of the basic parts of the human digestive system and trace food's one-way journey from mouth to anus. The core idea is a processing pipeline in which food is progressively broken down so useful nutrients can be ABSORBED into the body and waste removed. Keep functions simple (mouth breaks up, oesophagus squeezes, stomach churns, small intestine absorbs nutrients, large intestine absorbs water, rectum/anus remove waste); defer enzymes and villi to later (KS3). The transitional insight is that the small intestine absorbs nutrients into the blood (not 'food just passes through') and that the stomach does not do all the work alone. US note: NGSS has no elementary PE naming digestive organs; body systems as interacting subsystems appear later (MS-LS1-3), so treat as UK-led.

activities.title: Journey of the food: drive the bite along the canal
feedback: If a learner stops the journey at the stomach, prompt: what happens to the food after the stomach? Trace mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → out.
If a learner says the stomach does all the work, point out that chewing starts in the mouth and most nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine.

If a learner cannot explain 'absorb', return to the small-intestine wall: the good bits cross into the blood so they can reach the whole body; if the small intestine could not absorb, you could eat plenty and still not feed your body.

Reinforce that the small intestine's main job is absorbing NUTRIENTS and the large intestine's main job is soaking up WATER from the leftovers. These are different main jobs, and 'small' does not mean less important.
activities.rationale: An interactive that lets a child advance the food and trigger each transformation makes the sequence and the change enacted rather than just labelled; animating nutrients crossing the intestine wall gives a concrete referent for the abstract word 'absorb'. A fixed diagram shows where organs are but does not itself display the progressive change, so a driveable or physically enacted version can add that dimension. Efficacy of the interaction itself is a design proposal, not source-validated.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 statutory requirement: 'describe the simple functions of the basic parts of the digestive system in humans'.

The basic parts of the digestive system and their simple functions for KS2: mouth/teeth and saliva begin breakdown, oesophagus moves food to the stomach, stomach churns and mixes food with acid, small intestine absorbs nutrients into the blood, large intestine absorbs water, rectum/anus remove waste.
learnerActions: Starting with a labelled body outline showing the alimentary canal as one continuous tube from mouth to anus, move a single bite of food step by step along the canal.
At the mouth, show teeth chopping the food smaller and saliva softening it; at the oesophagus, make the tube squeeze the food down (peristalsis); at the stomach, churn it into a mush.

At the small intestine, show tiny nutrient particles crossing the intestine wall and floating into red blood vessels — state in your own words that 'absorb' means the useful bits leave the tube and enter the body.
At the large intestine, show water being soaked up and the leftover waste becoming more solid before it exits at the rectum and anus.
Say aloud the one simple job of each organ as you pass through it.
activities.intendedInsight: Digestion is a one-way sequence of transformations, and 'absorb' means nutrients leave the gut and enter the blood to feed the whole body — food does not merely pass straight through unchanged.

activities.title: Hands-on breakdown and squeeze model
feedback: If a learner thinks food 'falls' down, revisit the tights squeeze: the tube moves the food even when it is horizontal.
Link back to the on-screen or diagram journey so the physical model and the named sequence match up.
activities.rationale: Physically enacting the transformations before labelling them grounds abstract organ functions in direct experience, and the swallowing-lying-down example directly targets the gravity misconception. Tactile and on-screen versions offer different experiences and can reinforce each other.
sourceClaims: The basic parts of the digestive system and their simple functions for KS2: mouth/teeth and saliva begin breakdown, oesophagus moves food to the stomach, stomach churns and mixes food with acid, small intestine absorbs nutrients into the blood, large intestine absorbs water, rectum/anus remove waste.
learnerActions: Mash a cracker or biscuit with a fork to act as 'teeth' breaking food up, then add a little water as 'saliva' to soften it.
Squeeze the mush along a leg of tights (or a flexible tube) to feel how muscles push food along — this is peristalsis, not food 'falling' by gravity.
Discuss why you can still swallow when lying down, since the oesophagus squeezes food along rather than relying on gravity.
Connect this mechanical breakdown to the parallel Y4 'types of teeth' topic, so the mouth and its teeth are understood as the first stage of digestion.
activities.intendedInsight: Mechanical breakdown and muscular squeezing (peristalsis) are physical processes you can enact; the oesophagus moves food by muscle, which is why swallowing works lying down.

activities.title: Label and locate the organs on a body outline
feedback: If a learner draws a single stomach bag, remind them the canal continues as long coiled intestines.
If the stomach is placed at the belly button, correct to the upper left.
Optional enrichment: a rotatable 3D torso can help appreciate how the long small intestine coils to pack inside the abdomen, though the core Y4 learning is the process and simple functions.
activities.rationale: Producing and labelling a diagram is part of the stated evidence of learning and addresses the 'one bag' and belly-button placement misconceptions. A 3D model is offered as optional spatial enrichment with its affordance (appreciating length and coiling) stated, not as a requirement.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 statutory requirement: 'describe the simple functions of the basic parts of the digestive system in humans'.
learnerActions: On a body outline, draw or label the alimentary canal as a continuous tube from mouth to anus with each organ in place.
Place the stomach in the upper left (not at the belly button) and show the small intestine as a long, coiled tube.
Write a one-line simple job beside each organ (mouth chews/softens; oesophagus squeezes; stomach churns; small intestine absorbs nutrients; large intestine absorbs water; rectum/anus remove waste).
Optionally, use a labelled tappable torso with myth-buster flaps (e.g. 'does the stomach do all the digesting?', 'where are nutrients absorbed?') to check the named functions.
activities.intendedInsight: The digestive organs form one long connected canal with correct positions, not a single 'bag' where all food sits.

activities.title: Order the journey and distinguish the two intestines
feedback: If a learner says the stomach absorbs nutrients, re-trace to the small intestine as the place where nutrients cross into the blood.
If a learner conflates the two intestines, restate the main jobs: small intestine = absorbs nutrients, large intestine = soaks up water from the leftovers.
Use the probe 'What does the small intestine do that the stomach doesn't?' to check the absorption idea specifically.
activities.rationale: Ordering and matching consolidate the sequence and simple functions and can expose misconceptions through targeted questions; these response tasks check understanding but, on their own, do not require the learner to construct and drive the transformations, so they complement the enactment activities.
sourceClaims: The basic parts of the digestive system and their simple functions for KS2: mouth/teeth and saliva begin breakdown, oesophagus moves food to the stomach, stomach churns and mixes food with acid, small intestine absorbs nutrients into the blood, large intestine absorbs water, rectum/anus remove waste.
learnerActions: Put the organs in the order food travels, from mouth to exit.
Match each organ to its simple job.
Answer: where are nutrients absorbed? (small intestine) and where is water absorbed? (large intestine).
Explain why the small intestine's job of absorbing nutrients matters: without it you could eat plenty and still not feed your body.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the sequence and separates the small intestine (nutrient absorption) from the large intestine (water absorption), surfacing the common conflation and the 'stomach absorbs everything' idea.

constraints: Keep functions SIMPLE and age-appropriate: no enzymes or villi detail at this stage (that is KS3).
Teach 'absorb' explicitly as nutrients leaving the tube and entering the blood, not food merely passing straight through.

Distinguish the small intestine (main job: absorbs nutrients) from the large intestine (main job: soaks up water from what is left, making the waste more solid) directly, as learners routinely conflate them; 'small' does not mean less important. Avoid saying the small intestine absorbs no water, because in fact it absorbs most of it.
Use accurate but child-friendly organ positions: stomach upper left (not belly button), intestines as a long coiled canal, not a single bag.
Ordering/matching/selection tasks check understanding of the sequence but do not require learners to independently construct or enact the transformations; pair them with enactment or production.

A labelled diagram or physical model are scaffolds for the process: the physical tights/cracker model approximates mechanical breakdown and peristalsis and should be linked back to the named organ sequence.
US note: there is no elementary NGSS PE naming digestive organs; treat as UK-led and note later US placement (MS-LS1-3).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

In the source, the BBC Bitesize functions claim and the NGSS placement claim are marked verified:false; only the DfE statutory requirement is marked verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

No source attests that the 2D interactive or the physical tights/cracker model is more effective than other media; such comparative/necessity framing from the original ('better than any static image', static image 'shows where organs are but not the food being progressively changed') has been softened to affordance-based language. A fixed diagram can still support learning.
The original claim that open dialogue 'adds little to the core learning' is a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; it was omitted rather than propagated as a universal claim.

sourceClaims on activities 0, 1 and 4 cite content/standards claims that match the exact functions those activities teach; they anchor the content, not the efficacy of the interaction, which remains unvalidated.

probeDeeper: What does the small intestine do that the stomach doesn't?
Where does the water get taken out, so the waste becomes more solid?
Put the organs in the right order from mouth to exit.
If the small intestine couldn't absorb nutrients, what would happen even if you ate plenty?
assess.correctAnswer: After the mouth (chewing) and oesophagus, food reaches the stomach (which churns and breaks it down), then passes into the small intestine, where the useful nutrients are ABSORBED into the blood; what's left goes to the large intestine, where water is absorbed and waste is formed before it leaves the body. The small intestine's job — absorbing nutrients — is what lets the food actually feed the body.

errorPatterns.pattern: food goes into one 'tummy' bag and stays there until it comes out as waste
errorPatterns.nextMove: trace the full path mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine using a diagram
errorPatterns.distractor: It stays in the stomach until it comes out as waste
errorPatterns.revealedBy: stops the journey at the stomach, with no intestines

errorPatterns.pattern: digestion happens only in the stomach
errorPatterns.nextMove: spread the process along the tract — chewing, stomach breakdown, then intestinal absorption
errorPatterns.revealedBy: credits the stomach with the whole job

errorPatterns.pattern: nutrients aren't absorbed into the body — food just passes through
errorPatterns.nextMove: highlight the small intestine absorbing nutrients into the blood so they reach the whole body
errorPatterns.revealedBy: on the probe cannot say the small intestine absorbs nutrients into the blood

errorPatterns.pattern: the stomach makes the waste / waste is stored in the stomach
errorPatterns.nextMove: assign water absorption and waste formation to the large intestine
errorPatterns.revealedBy: locates waste formation in the stomach

responseLevels.gap: Stops the journey at the stomach, or thinks food just sits then leaves; cannot order the organs.
responseLevels.full: Names the digestive organs in order, explains each function including nutrient absorption in the small intestine and water absorption and waste formation in the large intestine, and traces the whole journey.
responseLevels.partial: Names the organs and some functions, but as a list — cannot explain the sequence, or that the small intestine absorbs nutrients into the blood.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: When you swallow a mouthful of food, some people think it just drops into your tummy and sits there until it comes out as waste. Trace where the food really goes after the stomach, and explain what the small intestine does that's so important.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the stomach is the end point (one bag) says food just sits and then leaves; a child who knows the journey continues to the intestines, and that nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine, explains the sequence and the absorption. The reason tier surfaces the 'one tummy' idea.
